book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

scenes.title: Different words. A possible bridge.
scenes.claim: Learnt representations can connect texts without shared terms
scenes.narration: Imagine two islands. On one: delulu job expectations. On the other: unrealistic career hopes. Their words differ, but a useful search system might connect them. Embeddings offer a bridge: compare learnt representations of the texts, rather than requiring shared terms.

scenes.title: A location made of numbers
scenes.claim: A vector is an ordered list; an embedding comes from a learnt mapping
scenes.narration: An encoder turns text into an ordered list of numbers: a vector. An embedding is a mapping into a vector space, usually learnt from data. We also call its output an embedding. Our two-dimensional maps are cartoons of spaces with hundreds or thousands of dimensions.

scenes.title: Both routes do arithmetic
scenes.claim: Specified weighting formula versus a mapping fitted during training
scenes.narration: BM twenty-five also calculates numbers, using term counts, lengths, and collection statistics in a specified formula. A neural encoder calculates its output using learnt parameters. The distinction is where the mapping comes from. A learnt mapping is still a calculation, not magic.

scenes.title: The text supplies the answer
scenes.claim: Similar contexts can supply a useful training signal
scenes.narration: But who labels the meaning of every word? The distributional hypothesis offers a practical shortcut: words used in similar contexts tend to be used in similar ways. Hide part of a sentence, predict it, and compare with the original. The text supplies its own target.

scenes.title: Two prediction games
scenes.claim: CBOW: context → word; Skip-gram: word → context
scenes.narration: Word two vec plays two versions of this game. Continuous bag of words predicts a word from its neighbours. Skip-gram predicts surrounding words from a word. Repeated errors adjust the parameters. After training, we keep the word vectors and use their geometry for other tasks.

scenes.title: Sometimes a direction is reusable
scenes.claim: Schematic analogy: king − man + woman ≈ queen; not a guarantee
scenes.narration: A famous demonstration subtracts man from king and adds woman. In some trained spaces, queen is nearest the result, excluding the input words. Similar relationships can share a direction. This drawing is schematic: it illustrates the idea, not measurements from a real model.

scenes.title: A picture is a shadow
scenes.claim: Illustrative coordinates; projection can hide high-dimensional structure
scenes.narration: Country-to-capital demonstrations show another reusable direction. But selected examples do not establish a universal rule. A two-dimensional projection is only a shadow of the full space. Individual dimensions are generally not labelled meaning, occupation, or age; patterns are spread across many coordinates.

scenes.title: Training chooses the compass
scenes.claim: Nearness reflects rewarded patterns; it does not certify relevance
scenes.narration: The key idea is that training decides which relationships the geometry tends to preserve. Co-occurrence can create useful regularities, but closeness does not certify that a passage answers your question. Next, we visit a word with two very different homes: bank.

scenes.title: The bank has two addresses
scenes.claim: The river bank and the bank refused the loan
scenes.narration: A traveller arrives at a bank carrying a fishing rod. Another arrives carrying a loan application. Same spelling, different context. The river bank and the bank refused the loan should not be represented as if their surrounding words supplied no information.

scenes.title: One stored vector per word
scenes.claim: Classic Word2Vec gives bank the same stored vector in both uses
scenes.narration: Classic word two vec stores one vector for bank. Both occurrences receive the same stored representation. That location can reflect mixed usage across the training corpus, but the lookup itself cannot choose a different vector for this particular river or this particular loan.

scenes.title: The neighbours change the result
scenes.claim: Contextual representations are computed for each occurrence
scenes.narration: A contextual encoder computes a representation for each occurrence from the sequence around it. River changes the evidence available to bank. Refused and loan change it differently. The starting token embedding is transformed into a contextual token representation. Our moving dots illustrate that change.

scenes.title: Words exchange information
scenes.claim: Self-attention lets token representations draw on other tokens
scenes.narration: A Transformer's self-attention lets a token's representation draw on other tokens in the sequence. Contextual representations also existed in recurrent systems such as ELMo. Transformers made this processing more parallelisable and scalable. Architecture tells us how information can flow, not what training rewards.

scenes.title: Two different kinds of small piece
scenes.claim: Model tokens and lexical index terms come from different processes
scenes.narration: Be careful with the small pieces. A lexical analyser produces terms for an index. A model tokenizer produces units the model reads, which can include subword pieces. They are different processes. This character-level toy split illustrates the distinction; it is not a named model's tokenization.

scenes.title: Many token vectors. One text vector.
scenes.claim: Pooling or a selected representation produces a complete-text vector
scenes.narration: Contextual token vectors are not yet one embedding for a complete query or passage. A retrieval encoder needs a way to produce that single vector. Pooling can combine token representations, or a model can use a selected representation. The choice depends on the model and its training.

scenes.title: Now the texts can be compared
scenes.claim: Compatible encoder outputs + a comparison rule → a score
scenes.narration: Encode the query and a passage with compatible mappings. A comparison rule can now score their vectors. There need not be a direct word match. But the score inherits the relationships learnt during training; it is not automatically a probability, a truth check, or a relevance judgement.

scenes.title: Context gives information. Training gives purpose.
scenes.claim: Contextualisation alone does not create a retrieval objective
scenes.narration: Context helps separate uses of bank and represent a whole sequence. It supplies information a model could use. It does not, by itself, tell the model to rank answers above merely related text. To understand that difference, we need to look at what the model was trained to predict.

episodes.title: Language knowledge is not relevance
episodes.subtitle: Pretraining, domain knowledge, and retrieval training

scenes.title: A sentence becomes its own quiz
scenes.claim: Self-supervised examples obtain their targets from text
scenes.narration: The patient received heart treatment after the attack. Hide part of that sentence, and the missing text becomes a training target. Nobody needs to write a separate answer key. Several language-learning objectives use this idea, but they give the model different evidence and different prediction tasks.

scenes.title: Game one: the neighbouring words
scenes.claim: Word2Vec CBOW predicts a word from a local context window
scenes.narration: In the continuous bag of words arrangement of word two vec, hide heart and predict it from a local window of neighbouring words. This is the CBOW illustration, not all of word two vec: Skip-gram reverses the prediction direction, from a word to its context.

scenes.title: Game two: read on both sides
scenes.claim: BERT: masked-token prediction using bidirectional context
scenes.narration: In masked language modelling, hide treatment. BERT can use context on both sides to predict that token. Learning this task develops broad language patterns. It does not directly teach independently encoded questions and relevant passages to land near each other.

scenes.title: Game three: the future stays hidden
scenes.claim: GPT-style next-token prediction uses only preceding tokens
scenes.narration: In next-token prediction, show the sentence only through treatment, and predict after. Everything to the right stays hidden; otherwise the model could read the answer. These GPT-style models learn to continue text from the left. Our word boxes simplify tasks that operate on model tokens.

scenes.title: Knowing language is not knowing the ranking
scenes.claim: Generic BERT is not automatically a useful first-stage retriever
scenes.narration: A model can be good at filling blanks and still produce poor search embeddings. BERT's pretraining objective gives it no direct requirement to arrange separate questions and answering passages for retrieval. Sentence-BERT changes the architecture and training to make complete-text representations useful for comparison.

scenes.title: A specialist library changes the background
scenes.claim: Domain pretraining changes language knowledge; task training changes purpose
scenes.narration: Domain pretraining is another lever. BioBERT continues pretraining on biomedical literature. BiomedBERT and SciBERT learn from domain-focused text and vocabulary. That changes their language background. It does not, by itself, decide what should rank first: retrieval-oriented training is still needed.

scenes.title: Reward the relationship you need
scenes.claim: Retrieval signals may be human, behavioural, weak, synthetic, or self-supervised
scenes.narration: Retrieval training supplies examples that reward the desired relationship. Its signal may come from human judgements, behaviour, weak or synthetic labels, or self-supervised pairs. In this cartoon, a question and a useful passage move closer. Actual training and its negatives determine how well that generalises.

scenes.title: Ask two questions about the model
scenes.claim: Was it trained for retrieval? Where does it sit in the pipeline?
scenes.narration: When a product says it uses BERT, ask two questions. Was the model trained for retrieval? And where does it sit in the pipeline: query interpretation, first-stage retrieval, or reranking? Training gives the map its purpose. Chapter six turns that map into comparable query and document embeddings.
